notes.text: As a rule, hold back f6 until you have castled; only a real emergency is an exception.
With the c-pawn break done, the f6 break against the e5 pawn is what you aim for later.
Typically you play knight e7, castle and then f6, while White eyes a4 and Ba3.
You can also play c6 and wait for White's reply before committing.
White develops a piece instead of taking the centre, which invites you to play a Sicilian-style ...c5.
Taking the pawn breaks White's center, but purists dislike it: you must play Nd7 and Ngf6, and your light bishop gets stuck.
White offers a bishop trade, which leads to a simpler, less complicated position.
Slide your queen to c7 to avoid any nasty tactics.
White's c4 hits your d5 pawn; taking is suicide while undeveloped, so close the center with d4.
Take the bishop; after the queen recaptures, your f6 pawn undermines e5 and White is in trouble.
Take the pawn; White's d-pawn is now isolated and stays a weakness.
This transposes into the Nimzowitsch system of the Advance French.
White's pawn kicks your bishop; you take on c3, then capture the pawn on e4.
The Orthoschnapp Gambit is unsound, which shows how tough the French is to meet.
A fun sideline: b6 and Ba6 swap your bad light bishop for White's good one, though it's dubious.
Your bishop takes the knight on h4, but be careful that it doesn't get trapped there.
Your knight on h6 heads for a good outpost.
White gains space with e5, so you must break his center with the c-pawn and f-pawn.
White's queen hits g7; you may give up a pawn for initiative and quick development.
The Exchange Variation is White's simplest try against the French, perhaps aiming for an improvised London setup.
Your light bishop is bad, blocked by your own pawn chain, so look to reroute it.
Taking your knight doesn't endanger your king; the opened g-file helps you attack White's king instead.
You are faster on the kingside; f6 and g5 matter most, but it is not yet won.
You gave back the pawn for the bishop pair and better development; Black is slightly better.
Bb5 check is fine for White; equality is expected, and trading bishops rids you of your bad bishop.
You pile up on the e5 pawn, and White must keep it defended or suffer.
White will push e5 soon, so you must exchange your d pawn now or be too late.
Taking on a3 lets White swap dark bishops, and Nb5 can't be stopped because a pawn is pinned.
You keep to mainline French moves while White prepares Nd2 for a King's Indian Attack setup.
Nf3 is the main line: White simply develops a piece and builds from there.
The French looks passive, but your light bishop can be useful, and c5 and f6 are your key breaks.
Your knight keeps the pressure on d4; taking on c5 or c6 would help you, not White.
A thematic White move: the bishop lines up on h7, creating mate threats.
White exchanging central pawns helps you; you now have a powerful central pawn formation.
This natural-looking knight move actually loses a pawn, because White continues with Bg5.
Nc3 develops, but with the c-file closed there is no Winawer, so you must free your light bishop.
White develops peacefully; as a French player, avoid symmetry rather than copying with Nf6.
Your play is mostly on the queenside, so don't castle right away; a kingside attack would be dangerous.
Your queen backs the d6 bishop, stopping a bishop trade and keeping the diagonal toward h2 under pressure.
An unusual surprise weapon that disrupts the usual French, though it is not thought as sound as d4.
White wasted time and gave up its centre; develop your knight, since e5 and c5 are weak.
White can grab the g7 pawn with the queen.
Or White can simply develop the knight to f3; both options are good.
Retake with your bishop on c5; it works with your queen against f2.
Taking on c3 is your only move; retreating the bishop lets White gain a strong initiative with b4.
Develop your g8 knight to e7 instead of rushing to grab pawns.
Your knight threatens Na5, forking White's queen and bishop.
White hopes you play f6 here, which loses material; just develop instead.
The engines like d4, but it's complicated: you must handle your weak central pawns or the center collapses.
White is better developed and your bishop and rooks are passive; Nb4 on move nine keeps you calmer.
White switches to his usual King's Indian setup, and you can aim at it with your center pawns.
Qb6 is equally good, but Bd7 keeps tension on White's light bishop.
White's queen blocks your e-pawn; keep pressing on the f-file and the diagonal toward f2.
Your c4 advance only works once White's queenside pawns have moved, as here.
Nd7 is a favorite here: it often transposes to Caro-Kann Karpov ideas and needs little study.
Your knight hits the bishop on c2; if White gives up that bishop, the pressure on your kingside drops.
One idea is to reroute your bad light bishop toward f7 so it stops being a problem piece.
Your d-pawn hits the bishop on c4 and challenges White's centre.
Usually f6 waits until you have castled, but White's passive setup can't punish it here.
The Kasparov Attack: c3 protects the d4 pawn and clears the way for the queen to go to a4.
This move defines the French: very solid, but your light bishop needs careful development.
You're slightly better: your big pawn center gives you play, so keep pushing it.
Just develop: bishop to e7, knight to f6, castle short, and you are roughly fine.
If White advances e5, you hit d4 with c5, Nc6 and Qb6 to undermine White's centre.
Qe2 is an unusual move that has fallen out of favor, since White normally prefers Nf3, g3 and Bg2.
Your pawn in the centre transposes to a proper French: Paulsen after d4, or Two Knights after Nf3.
White simply waits to see what you do: either you advance the pawn or exchange.
You invite a knight trade; Nd7 first lets you retake with that knight, so your kingside pawns stay intact.
Your c5 and f6 pawns challenge White's centre on both wings, so White can't attack quickly.
This is the Advance Variation of the French.
White's c3 pawn protects the d4 pawn; if you take on d4 and White retakes with the pawn, it becomes isolated.
White pins your knight to the queen; simply defend with your bishop and carry on.
Taking on e4 does not give up the center: you will hit it with c5 and fight for it.
White wants to fianchetto its blocked light bishop, which is a respectable idea.
In the Perseus gambit, if you take on e4 and White's knight reaches e5, ...f6 loses to a queen check.
White's f4 is playable, but it loosens the dark squares around its own kingside.
White wants more control of the center, and this could grow into a Bird-style setup.
White's pawn guards d4; trading on d4 and retaking with the pawn leaves White an isolated pawn.
Bring your queen to b6 to pressure the center.
Your knight hits the bishop on c2, aiming to get rid of White's bishop pair.
Castle, improve your pieces, then start a queenside pawn attack; the overextended e5 pawn is also a target.
With pawns on c4 and e4, White's d-pawn lacks pawn support, which makes it a target.
Your f6 challenges the center at once, but it weakens your light squares; g6 can patch them.
You may keep the extra pawn, but White's knight gets strong counterplay with the d6 square.
c3 is one of White's best replies, holding up the overextended d4 pawn.
Another trap: you keep building the attack, and every White move is risky.
Your counterplay aims at g2 down the g-file, or you can push c5.
Exchanging the pawns only leads to simplification.
You have a strong attack on White's kingside.
Simply develop your other knight and your game will be much easier.
White gains space with e5, but the game is about to get messy.

This game ended in a win for White.

You are a clean pawn up, which should be enough for an advantage.
White's c4 gains space but gives up pawn protection, and you benefit most from it.
Qe2 invites an exchange on e4, but that allows a check on b5; White's bishop still reaches g2.
Nd2 stops your Winawer pin; just trade pawns on e4 and keep things simple.
Play f6 to support your center pawns.
Let go of the center and get on with the game.
White's queen had to come out; a bishop to b4 would pin the d2 knight.
The natural reply: if White takes on d5, your knight recaptures and lands in the center.
This is the Tarrasch: solid and the most played, giving White a sturdy center while you attack it.
Rare idea: Bd7, take on d4, then Bb5 to swap bishops, at the cost of your queenside structure.
Your knight belongs on g6; White is planning queen to e2.
Your king is in great danger here; White has a strong attack and your position may crumble.
Many opening traps arise from this position, and White's b4 is already complicated.
Remember, the c5 break is mandatory if you want to play for a win.
White's broken queenside and slow development let you win the pawns back.
White plays a3 to prepare b4, which opens the queenside and undermines your d4 pawn.
Push g5 soon and keep your c and d pawns connected; castle long, not short.
Be2 is a less provocative choice for White, safe rather than sorry.
Your knight starts a strong attack on White's kingside, which White will find hard to handle.
White can sidestep the classical French with Nf3, but it usually transposes after Nc3, so we follow that.
White's usual c3 steadies the d4 pawn and opens the queen's diagonal toward a4.
Here you are fine with good counterplay, but you must remember the key Rb8 and h5 moves.

This is the Alekhine Gambit: you can grab the pawn on e4, but keep things simple.
Strike the center with c5 to break up White's central pawns.
White's c3 pawn supports the center by guarding the d4 pawn.
White next plays Rh7, forcing Rf7, which would be very unpleasant for your stuck king.
The Rubinstein is a simple way to meet this line, and White has little pressure on the center.
White's pawn kicks your bishop; retreat it to keep the bishop pair.
You need to castle fast; think about how to make up for the lost tempo.
Knight c6 is the preferred reply: simple, it threatens dxc4 and pressures the d4 pawn.

This knight move has little independent value, since it transposes into other opening lines.
Your rook prepares the f6 break, challenging White's e5 pawn.
A drawish position; to win it you must exploit White's doubled c-pawns and weak a-pawn.
A very common French sacrifice: you give a rook for initiative and active pieces.
Hit White's e5 pawn with f6 once you have castled; it works, but carries some risk.
White avoids the French and plans a slow setup; the fight will be over the e-pawn.
Nc6 is the usual main line; develop your bishop to d7 and knight to e7 next.
One possible continuation: in the main line White gives away a pawn here.
This transposes to an Advance French; aim for your standard French setup, adjusting if needed.
You are ready to give up material for a tactic against White's exposed king.
You must castle now, then develop your light bishop and open the f-file.

Keep it simple: take the pawn on e4 and your life gets much easier.

White gives up a pawn for now but expects to win it back soon.

White can save only one pawn, e5 or c5; keeping the e5 pawn is much better.

You have very good play and the bishop pair.
White keeps developing pieces. You can answer with ...Nf6, or gain space by pushing ...d4 to kick the knights.

An unorthodox try: White prepares Bg2 to challenge your light bishop before it settles on b7.

h3 stops Ng4, but your knight can go to h5, and White's dark squares get weak.

The most common reply: your knight keeps pressure on the e4 pawn.

This game ended in a win for White.

The most aggressive move: sooner or later White must open the f-file or the c-file.

A precise move: it defends the d4 pawn and prepares b4 sooner.
